articles.title: Powerful Thanksgiving storms knockout power, disrupt East Coast travel
articles.summary: Thanksgiving storms left more than 800,000 reported outages as high winds, flooding and travel disruptions swept the United States.
articles.body:
For millions of people around the country, Thanksgiving 2026 brought travel headaches, powerful storms and power outages.

Forecasters with the National Weather Service said poor weather was expected through Nov. 27 for much of the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast. Travelers taking to the roads and skies were advised to check conditions.

"Heavy rain, damaging winds, and coastal flooding will continue through the afternoon and evening hours across portions of the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast leading to moderate to major impacts over the region," the weather service said in an afternoon forecast. "Coastal flooding is ongoing across much of the Mid-Atlantic coast."

Powerful Thanksgiving storm brings wind damage and parade delays

Earlier on Nov. 26, the storm stretched from St. Louis east to New York City and Boston, as far south as Nashville, and was closing in on Buffalo, New York. AAA projected 81.5 million people would travel at least 50 miles from home during the holiday period.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a preemptive state of emergency for New York City, and Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester counties. In New York City, gusts reached 40 mph .

Parts of southeastern Missouri saw as much as 14 inches of snow between Nov. 25 and Thanksgiving morning, according to the National Weather Service in St. Louis. More than two inches of snow fell in Columbia, Missouri, with the weather service reporting it was the snowiest Thanksgiving morning in the city in more than two decades and the "biggest Thanksgiving snowstorm" in nearly 50 years.

St. Louis saw more than seven inches of snow, an increase from a 6.4-inch snowfall in 2025, the weather service said . It marks the first time on record that the city has "recorded a top 10 November snowfall in back to back years."

The Wentzville Ice Arena, northwest of St. Louis, collapsed in the storm and will remain closed "until further notice," officials said .

Over 800,000 power outages reported across US

USA TODAY's power outage tracker showed growing power losses in coastal Virginia, particularly around Newport News and Williamsburg, and also in St. Louis and the surrounding suburbs. Videos posted to social media showed street flooding in parts of eastern Virginia.

More than 800,000 power outages had been reported nationwide as of 10:46 p.m. ET, largely centered in Missouri and the East Coast. In Maryland, officials closed the Bay Bridge to travel in both directions, and live traffic cameras bounced in the wind and rain.

Storm affecting Maryland water treatment plants

The Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission asked nearly two million customers in Maryland's Montgomery and Prince George's counties to "immediately conserve water" because the storm was causing "intermittent power disruptions" at water treatment plants in the Washington metro area.

The commission asked residents to use water only for essential purposes to "preserve water for fire protection and system storage." In a 6 p.m. ET update, the commission said the request remained in effect throughout both counties.

Both the Potomac and Patuxent water filtration plants had power and were producing drinking water at that time, the commission said, adding that they may still "experience storm-related interruptions."

The commission asked residents to take measures including taking shorter showers and limiting use of washing machines and dishwashers. Taking such measures "could help preserve water for system storage and fire protection until the storm passes and power reliability is restored," the statement said.

Landspout tornado possible southeast of Seattle

The National Weather Service in Seattle said Thanksgiving afternoon that a landspout tornado and penny-sized hail were possible in areas southeast of Seattle, including Auburn, Palmer and Cedar Falls.

The weather service's statement was set to expire at 1:45 p.m. local time.

A tornado warning was issued earlier to areas including Issaquah and North Bend, Washington.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani urged both residents and visitors alike to be safe as the storm approached the Big Apple. The Macy's parade was rescheduled to 8:30 a.m. ET on Nov. 28. The parade's delay set off a scramble for high school bands and other performers to find places to stay during the year's busiest travel period.

As of 3 p.m. ET, winds in Central Park were 20 mph with gusts of 41 mph, the weather service reported. Winds were expected to strengthen later in the day, with gusts of up to 65 mph. The weather service predicted "widespread" power outages and said high-profile vehicles could get blown over.

Parade organizers cited the poor weather in delaying the parade by two days, noting the popular large-scale balloons could pose a risk to handlers and crowds in high winds.

"If you are planning to travel, budget extra time and remember that no destination is worth your safety," Mamdani said in a social media post . "Never walk or drive through flooding. If winds pick up, go inside. These are winds strong enough to down tree limbs and power lines — so be sure to secure outdoor furniture, trash cans, and holiday decorations ahead of time."

Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed. Revisit 2025's floats

Air travelers facing delays, cancellations

Most airlines issued travel waivers to passengers and reminded flyers to check for delays and cancellations.

As of 8 p.m. ET, there were 2,295 delays and 1,207 cancellations for U.S. flights, according to FlightAware's Misery Map . Baltimore/Washington International Airport had the most cancellations at that time, with 48 outbound and 46 inbound flights cancelled.

JFK International in New York, Boston's Logan International, and Miami International were also suffering significant delays and cancellations, according to FlightAware. Washington Dulles International Airport was experiencing departure delays averaging more than one hour as of 8 p.m. ET.

Department of Transportation rules require airlines to offer travelers a refund if their flight is canceled for any reason, regardless of ticket type, if they choose not to fly. If they choose to continue their trip, they are entitled to penalty-free rebooking on the same airline.

If a cancellation is outside of the airline's control – as is the case with inclement weather – the only thing travelers are owed is rebooking or a refund.

In California, dangerous coastal conditions persisted. The weather service warned of moderate to major coastal flooding in the San Francisco area, with a risk of unexpected "sneaker" waves of 13-19 feet high in some areas.

The weather service said people in the San Francisco area should expect some road closures and flooding of low-lying areas through 4 p.m. Pacific Time. A portion of the Pacifica Pier near San Francisco collapsed as it was battered by high waves on Nov. 25.
authors: Trevor Hughes and BrieAnna J. Frank, USA TODAY

articles.title: Israeli settlers damage Palestinian family’s homes in West Bank attack
articles.summary: The Tubasi family was forced out months ago and has been denied a return by settlers despite an Israeli court order.
articles.body:
Israeli settlers have smashed the foundations of two homes belonging to a Palestinian family in the occupied West Bank after attacks stopped the family from returning.

Security cameras showed the settlers bringing a bulldozer to the two-storey houses in the village of Jaloud, near Nablus, at about 1am on Thursday (23:00 GMT on Wednesday), before starting to damage them, Reuters reported. It added that the concrete foundations of the homes had been partially broken.

“This latest escalation is a direct consequence of the lack of law enforcement and the sense of impunity enjoyed by the perpetrators,” said Ghiath Nasser, the owners’ lawyer.

The Israeli military said the attack was “a serious criminal act” and said it was investigating, despite settlers remaining in the vicinity throughout the day.

The Tubasi family now live in a small house in Jaloud with a direct view of the homes they fled. “They want to demolish the houses so that we cannot return to them,” Wael Tubasi, one of the owners, said.

He said the deadline for the military to remove the settlers had passed.

“Even though there is a court order, and the army is required to remove them from the area entirely, not just return us to our homes, it’s still not being implemented,” he said.

The family said settlers set up a tent near their homes in April and began attacking them. They said settlers set fire to the homes, cut their water and electricity and blocked the roads.

After three months, settlers told the family they had an hour to leave or be killed “like the Dawabsheh family”, Wael’s mother, Aedah, said. In 2015, settlers set fire to the Dawabsheh family’s home in the village of Duma, killing an 18-month-old child and both his parents.

In September, soldiers escorted the family back to their homes under the court order. Ten minutes later, about 200 settlers attacked them, forcing the family and the soldiers to retreat, the family said. The settlers then burned the homes and broke much of the furniture.

“I’m forbidden from reaching my home, while the settlers have the right to remain inside. What rights are there?” Aedah said.

The attack follows weeks of settler pogroms across the occupied West Bank. There have been an average of 53 settler attacks a week since the start of the year, according to the UN. The agency said on November 20 that more than 400 settler attacks causing casualties or damage had been recorded since September, more than in any previous season .

Over the weekend, settlers set fire to at least a dozen vehicles and several homes in five villages, and sprayed “Revenge” on walls. Last week, settlers killed an elderly Palestinian woman and wounded 10 other people in a pogrom near Jericho .

According to the Israeli rights group Yesh Din, 93.6 percent of investigations into settler pogroms are closed without indictments.

articles.title: A South African father and son spent months developing a 3D-printed racing drone in their workshop; their fourth-generation Peregreen quadcopter has now achieved an officially recognised average speed of 408 mph
articles.summary: A father-and-son engineering project started in a workshop in South Africa has reached extraordinary heights, turning a home-built flying machine into a
articles.body: A father-and-son engineering project started in a workshop in South Africa has reached extraordinary heights, turning a home-built flying machine into a world record-breaking speed machine. After months of motor tweaking, 3D printing parts and aerodynamic engineering, brothers Mike and Luke Bell have taken their fourth-generation Peregreen quadcopter to an officially recognized average speed of 408.60 mph (657.59 km/h), taking the crown as the world's fastest battery-powered remote-controlled quadcopter. According to Futura Sciences, the achievement was recorded on December 11, 2025 in Cape Town, the latest milestone in the duo's years-long quest for speed records with drones.From workshop experiment to world record holderAccording to the online reports, the Bells have been working with quadcopters for generations, each one more advanced than the last. Their Peregreen 2 hit 298 mph (480 km/h) and was recognized by Guinness World Records in 2024. In October 2025, the father-and-son team set another record with Peregreen 3, achieving an average speed of about 363 mph (585 km/h), the report adds.But it wasn’t long before their success was undone. That record was then taken from the South African builders by the Black Bird quadcopter designed by Australian aerospace engineer Benjamin Biggs, who is known online as Drone Pro Hub, with an average speed of 389 mph (626 km/h).The Bells were already working on their next generation aircraft, preparing for their return to the top, Cape Town ETC reports.Upgrade is led by 3D printing and engineeringPeregreen V4 is the result of five months of intensive testing and design enhancements, MyBroadband reports. The team worked to minimize aerodynamic drag, while ensuring the aircraft could withstand the stresses of ultra high speed flight.A larger 3D printer enabled them to build a bigger frame, and sanded surfaces helped improve airflow around the aircraft.A major upgrade was the fitting of aerodynamic streamliners around the propeller bases. These 3D printed parts were designed to reduce turbulence and increase efficiency.The Bells also ran computational fluid dynamics simulations to tweak the drone’s body. After testing various motors they settled on four T-Motor 3120s rated at 900 kV, with a focus on reliability and lower operating temperatures.The new design of the propeller spinners underwent a series of rigorous bench tests, standing up to speeds over 70,000 revolutions per minute.A second drone to film the record-breaking flightAnother challenge was the recording of the airplane. The speed of the flight was so great that ordinary cameras had trouble taking clear pictures.MyBroadband report adds that the team also built a second drone specifically to film the record attempts. They mounted an Insta360 X5 camera in a custom 3D-printed tail section, which allows them to reframe the footage after the flight.The official record attempt involved four runs in opposite directions to account for wind conditions and get a reliable average speed.Taking back the crownAs Futura Sciences points out, the Peregreen V4 was able to reach speeds of about 656 km/h in one direction and 659 km/h in the other. The Guinness World Records clocked it at an average speed of 657.59 km/h (408.60 mph).The achievement was around 31 km/h faster than the previous record, bringing the title back to the South African duo.Getaway stressed the importance of the feat for Cape Town where the home-built aircraft did its record-setting runs.The Bells’ latest achievement adds another chapter to the growing race to build the world’s fastest racing drone, as every generation of the Peregreen demonstrates how independent engineering and 3D printing can challenge the limits of technology.Images Courtesy: New Atlas and Luke Maximo BellYou use AI every day. articles.body:

A chuva registrada entre quarta-feira (25) e quinta-feira (26) provocou oito ocorrências em Maricá , na Região Metropolitana do Rio.

Entre os atendimentos realizados pela Defesa Civil estão problemas em estruturas, erosão de via e alagamentos. Uma família precisou ser encaminhada para um abrigo após uma residência ser atingida pela água.

De acordo com a prefeitura, duas ocorrências de movimentação de terra foram registradas em Itaipuaçu. Também houve desprendimento de material de uma encosta no Centro e problemas em um muro de contenção em São José do Imbassaí.

Em Cordeirinho, foi registrado o desabamento parcial de um teto. Já em Itapeba, houve erosão em uma via. Em Chácaras de Inoã, uma residência foi atingida por alagamento e uma família precisou ser encaminhada para um abrigo.

No Jardim Atlântico Central, em Itaipuaçu, os alagamentos foram provocados pelo transbordamento do canal da Rua Professor Cardoso de Menezes, antiga Rua 1, segundo a prefeitura.

A Defesa Civil também atendeu a uma ocorrência de risco de transbordamento de rio. Como medida preventiva, as equipes interditaram parcialmente uma via e uma edificação.

Segundo a prefeitura, os agentes continuam monitorando as condições meteorológicas, vistoriando as áreas afetadas e atendendo às ocorrências.

articles.body:

Uma visita em família a um cemitério em Praia Norte , no norte do Tocantins, divertiu internautas nas redes sociais. O motivo foi uma conversa descontraída entre uma avó, a mãe e as tias sobre os espaços reservados para o sepultamento dos parentes.

O registro foi feito no dia 7 de novembro pela enfermeira e criadora de conteúdo Thaislane Rithele de Sousa, de 29 anos. Na gravação, aparecem a avó, a mãe, cinco tias e uma criança, todas em cima da área destinada aos familiares, debatendo quem ficará ao lado de quem no futuro.

Segundo Thaislane, a família foi ao cemitério a pedido da avó, que queria visitar o túmulo do marido, falecido em 2011. Durante a conversa, mãe e filha chegam a disputar quem terá o "privilégio" de ficar enterrada mais perto da matriarca.

"Minhas tias são exatamente daquele jeito. Inclusive, essa minha tia de vestido já tem o caixão pago e a roupa do enterro pronta", revelou.

articles.title: Prefeitura do Ceará sugere devolver em até 100 parcelas R$ 410 mil em impostos pagos por engano por contribuintes de cidade do Paraná | G1
articles.standfirst: Dinheiro deveria ter sido destinado à Prefeitura de Toledo, mas foi parar nas contas do município de Itaiçaba após erro no sistema de cobrança. Caso está na Justiça desde junho.
articles.summary: Dinheiro deveria ter sido destinado à Prefeitura de Toledo, mas foi parar nas contas do município de Itaiçaba após erro no sistema de cobrança. Caso está na Justiça desde junho.
articles.body:
Prefeitura de Toledo — Foto: Divulgação/Prefeitura

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

A Prefeitura de Itaiçaba, no Ceará, sugeriu devolver em até 100 parcelas os R$ 410 mil em impostos que foram parar por engano nas contas do município e deveriam ter sido destinados à Prefeitura de Toledo, no oeste do Paraná.

O dinheiro é referente à arrecadação do Imposto Sobre Serviços (ISS) e foi direcionado ao município cearense em janeiro deste ano, após um erro no sistema de cobrança de impostos.

Há quase um ano, a prefeitura paranaense tenta recuperar o valor. Após tentativas de negociação sem sucesso, a administração municipal entrou com uma ação judicial de cobrança em junho. O caso aguarda julgamento.

Caso a devolução seja feita em 100 parcelas mensais, sem considerar eventuais juros e correções monetárias, seriam necessários oito anos e quatro meses para quitar o valor , com pagamentos de aproximadamente R$ 4,1 mil por mês .

Segundo a Prefeitura de Toledo, o erro aconteceu durante uma mudança no modelo de cobrança bancária. Algumas guias de pagamento do imposto foram emitidas com o código de cobrança de Itaiçaba.

Com isso, ao pagarem o imposto, os contribuintes de Toledo destinaram o dinheiro diretamente ao município cearense.

"Não houve transferência ou PIX: o valor não entrou na conta da Prefeitura de Toledo, mas já entrou na conta da prefeitura cearense", explicou a administração municipal.

Ainda segundo a prefeitura paranaense, assim que o erro foi identificado, a administração entrou em contato com o município cearense, que inicialmente teria concordado em devolver o dinheiro.

No entanto, a devolução não aconteceu, mesmo após várias tentativas de negociação.

Em nota divulgada em 20 de novembro, a Prefeitura de Itaiçaba afirmou que não teve participação no erro que fez com que o dinheiro fosse direcionado às contas do município.

A administração municipal também argumentou que movimentações financeiras envolvendo recursos públicos precisam seguir procedimentos legais específicos, diferentes daqueles realizados entre particulares.

A prefeitura informou ainda que acompanha o processo judicial e destacou que um pedido de decisão provisória foi negado pela Justiça.

Na ocasião, o município cearense não informou se o dinheiro permanecia nas contas da prefeitura nem apresentou uma previsão para a devolução dos valores.

O Paraná tem 73 cidades sob alerta laranja, de perigo, para tempestade nesta sexta-feira (27), segundo o Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet).

O aviso é válido das 9h40 às 23h59 e prevê chuva de até 60 milímetros por hora, ventos de até 100 km/h e risco de alagamentos, queda de galhos de árvores, descargas elétricas e falta de energia. Veja lista de cidades abaixo.

De acordo com o Sistema de Tecnologia e Monitoramento Ambiental do Paraná (Simepar), o tempo continuará bastante instável principalmente no Oeste e Sudoeste, onde a chuva deve ocorrer em vários momentos e os acumulados podem ultrapassar 50 milímetros.

Ao longo da tarde e da noite, as instabilidades avançam para outras regiões do estado, com possibilidade de pancadas de chuva e temporais rápidos e isolados, especialmente no Noroeste.

Nuvem prateleira se forma em Foz do iguaçu — Foto: Roberto Lemos

Oeste e Sudoeste concentram maiores volumes de chuva

Alerta da climatempo para sexta-feira (27) — Foto: Climatempo

Segundo a Climatempo, a chuva deve perder força em parte do estado, mas ainda há previsão de pancadas moderadas a fortes em diferentes regiões.

O risco de temporais permanece maior no Oeste e no Norte do Paraná. Nas demais áreas, a chuva deve ocorrer de maneira mais irregular.

Entre os maiores volumes previstos estão Barracão, no Sudoeste, com aproximadamente 56 milímetros, e Ampére, com 45 milímetros.

As temperaturas continuam mais amenas em boa parte do estado. Segundo o Simepar, as mínimas ficam abaixo dos 15°C na Região Metropolitana de Curitiba, nos Campos Gerais e no Centro-Sul.

Durante a tarde, o calor aumenta no Norte e Noroeste, onde os termômetros podem chegar a 28°C e 29°C.

Em Curitiba, a previsão da Climatempo indica mínima de 13°C e máxima de 20°C. O dia começa com céu encoberto e possibilidade de garoa. À tarde, podem ocorrer aberturas de sol e pancadas de chuva, enquanto à noite a tendência é de melhora.

Como se proteger durante as chuvas intensas

O Inmet orienta que a população adote cuidados durante os períodos de chuva e rajadas de vento.

Não procure abrigo debaixo de árvores , devido ao risco de queda e descargas elétricas.

Evite estacionar veículos próximos a torres de transmissão e placas de propaganda .

Se possível, desligue aparelhos elétricos e o quadro geral de energia.

Em situações de emergência, entre em contato com a Defesa Civil pelo telefone 199 ou com o Corpo de Bombeiros pelo 193 .

A população também pode acompanhar os avisos meteorológicos atualizados no site oficial do Inmet.

articles.title: 'Como descobri que um desconhecido foi enterrado no túmulo que comprei | G1
articles.standfirst: Marie Lane levou mais de três anos para conseguir retirar o corpo de um desconhecido enterrado por engano no espaço que ela havia reservado no cemitério.
articles.summary: Marie Lane levou mais de três anos para conseguir retirar o corpo de um desconhecido enterrado por engano no espaço que ela havia reservado no cemitério.
articles.body:
Marie Lane diz que tem 'noites sem dormir' por causa do erro — Foto: BBC

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Uma mulher diz que não se sente mais da mesma forma em relação à sepultura que havia reservado e pago depois que um desconhecido foi enterrado no local por engano e, posteriormente, exumado.

Marie Lane, de 69 anos, havia reservado um terreno no cemitério de Deeping St James, uma pequena cidade no condado de Lincolnshire, no leste da Inglaterra, atrás das sepulturas de seus pais. Ela conta que se sentiu "bastante vazia" e "horrorizada" com a maneira como o conselho paroquial lidou com o erro.

No início deste ano, o Ministério da Justiça britânico autorizou a exumação da pessoa enterrada por engano no terreno, para que a área fosse devolvida a Lane.

O Conselho Paroquial de Deeping St James afirmou que "reconhece que houve um erro" e pediu desculpas "pelo sofrimento causado às duas famílias ". O órgão disse que o terreno foi devolvido a Lane.

Em 2013, Lane comprou o direito exclusivo de ser enterrada em um espaço no cemitério atrás da sepultura de sua mãe, segundo um documento do Conselho Paroquial de Deeping St James ao qual a BBC teve acesso.

"Comprei um terreno para ficar perto dos meus pais", disse Lane.

"Não faz sentido ser enterrada aqui se não puder ficar junto dos meus entes queridos."

No início de 2023, ao visitar o cemitério, ela descobriu que outra pessoa havia sido enterrada no espaço que havia reservado .

"Eu simplesmente fiquei parada ali, sem saber o que fazer, para ser sincera", lembra.

"Uma pessoa que eu não conheço foi enterrada na minha sepultura."

Lane levou mais de três anos para conseguir a autorização para retirar o corpo . Segundo ela, não havia "outra alternativa", já que não existiam outros espaços disponíveis nas proximidades das sepulturas de seus pais.

Na Inglaterra, a exumação de um corpo enterrado em área não consagrada exige autorização do Ministério da Justiça. Em geral, também é necessário o consentimento dos familiares mais próximos da pessoa falecida.

Em uma carta enviada ao Conselho Paroquial de Deeping St James, o ministério autorizou a exumação mesmo sem o consentimento dos familiares e apesar das objeções "morais e religiosas" apresentadas por eles.

A decisão foi justificada pela "falta de outras soluções possíveis" para "permitir que o erro fosse corrigido".

A BBC tentou entrar em contato com a família da pessoa exumada.

Eric Lane, de 77 anos, marido de Marie, disse que o episódio teve um "impacto devastador" sobre a esposa.

Ele afirmou acreditar que o conselho paroquial "não consegue manter registros adequados para evitar esse tipo de erro" e disse temer que algo semelhante volte a acontecer.

A BBC questionou o conselho sobre a acusação e perguntou quais medidas foram adotadas para evitar novos erros. O órgão não respondeu.

Eric disse que a esposa "não gosta" mais de visitar o cemitério.

"Há tanta maldade e amargura associadas a esse lugar que não sei se isso algum dia vai passar", afirmou.

Marie Lane disse que se solidariza com a família da pessoa enterrada por engano em seu terreno e que entende o sofrimento que eles enfrentaram.

"Eu pedi inúmeras vezes ao [conselho paroquial] que organizasse um encontro com eles, mas me disseram que não."

Marie Lane acrescentou: "Eu me sinto muito desconfortável até mesmo em visitar o cemitério. Não vamos nem perto do lugar com a mesma frequência de antes."

"Isso não deveria ter levado três anos e três meses, e não deveríamos ter precisado lutar dessa maneira", afirmou.

articles.title: Why there's a shortage of lift and escalator mechanics
articles.summary: The pay is good and there's lots of work, so what's behind the shortage of elevator mechanics?
articles.body:
Some of them are angry. Nerves are frayed. Many of them are just relieved that he's here.

When a lift stops working in Chicago, frazzled building managers might get a visit from Jim Lembesis. For more than 47 years, Lembesis has repaired and upgraded lifts. He says he understands why staff and residents are so anxious to have things working again.

"They wait and they wait," says Lembesis, a field technician for Parkway Elevators. "There's a lot of frustration. Sometimes it's a repeat issue. It's a never-ending cycle, you know what I mean?"

The widely reported shortage of lift and escalator mechanics in the US, which is also a problem in many other countries, has got worse over time, he adds: "It's been like night and day compared to when I started."

Everyone needs a lift now and again. Some people depend on them – elderly residents of high-rise buildings, say, or wheelchair users.

Storm-damaged lifts in Hawaiian apartment blocks this year left some residents trapped in their homes for weeks. A lack of mechanics, and problems sourcing parts, were blamed for the repair delays.

In the US, the average salary for a lift mechanic is $110,000 (£83,000). And yet people in the industry say it is difficult to attract new workers.

Sure, says Lembesis, you do encounter some dangers in a job like this. There are risks of falling from a great height – or being electrocuted. Once, he was even hit on the head with an umbrella by an elderly lady after he rescued her from a stuck lift.

But there are so many skills to learn, and great camaraderie and knowledge-sharing among mechanics, he says. As one recruiter puts it, these technicians amaze people with their ability to fix things. They are like "wizards". The overall-clad shamans who know how to get modern life running again.

Nine times out of 10, the problem is with the doors, says Lembesis. These components repeatedly move back and forth. "People hit them with carts, and dirt and debris [falls into them]," says Lembesis. "[The doors] take the most beating."

Mechanics often keep various spare door parts in their vehicles, ready to use.

But technicians like Lembesis don't just have to get lifts working, they also have to verify the lifts are safe. He remembers one case, decades ago, getting called out to a burning building. His role was to ensure the lifts, which were being drenched with huge volumes of water, were still safe to use while firefighters tackled the blaze.

"I was there for 15 hours that night," he says. "Everyone, on the way out of the door, shook my hand."

Finding good lift technicians is "becoming more difficult" says Matt Hollinshead, president of the US National Association for Elevator Contractors. "We have a four-year apprenticeship," he says. That's the first hurdle. And many states require certification or licensing before you can work on lifts.

"We have a vast array of equipment that has to be maintained in the United States." Some lifts are 100-years-old. As time goes on, the technological knowledge required to repair them only grows.

Hollinshead says that weeks or months-long delays to lift repairs are not typically due to staff shortages but that, in such cases, it's likely that a particular part isn't readily available. Manufacturing a replacement hydraulic cylinder takes six to 12 weeks, he notes.

But the lack of technicians does mean that that building managers might have to wait days before someone can even diagnose what's wrong with a lift after it stops working.

Hollinshead says teaching the basics of the trade in high schools or technical schools could entice more people into the role.

Matt Allred, a recruiter and host of The Elevator Careers Podcast, emphasises the many skills that lift mechanics require. "You're a little bit of a wizard, right? You show up and if you can fix it – 'Wow!'."

He blames major lift companies, in part, for locking down maintenance contracts, making it difficult or impossible for third-party repairers to intervene when a lift fails.

Two large lift manufacturers approached by BBC News declined interviews. The chief executive of Otis, one of the firms, said in May that her company was struggling to hire enough staff to meet demand. The firm also states on its website that the shortage of lift mechanics affects "almost every part of the world".

However, a spokesman for Otis claimed its "US talent pipeline" was healthy, and declined an interview.

Everyone else who spoke to BBC News said hiring was challenging in the US. Allred was recently contacted by a major lift company and asked to help them find a technician. "I was surprised that a major company would reach out to a little recruiting shop," he says, suggesting that this reflects the extent of the labour shortage.

That shortage is also a problem in the UK. "It is bad and getting worse," says Dave Cooper, president of the Chartered Institution of Building Services Engineers, who is also chief executive of a lift and escalator engineering consultancy.

"We've known food delivery companies to refuse to deliver to flats above the ground floor because the lift is out of service."

Offering better tax breaks to companies that train lift mechanics could help ensure that plenty of workers continue to enter the industry, he adds.

Training to be a lift mechanic is "not a quick route to competency – and it requires people to stick at it for the long term" says Karen Slade, head of assessment at the Lift and Escalator Industry Association (Leia).

Continued investment in training and attracting new workers is "essential", according to Leia. There are currently 259 active lift and escalator apprentices in the UK, the body adds.

Back in Chicago, Lembesis is working with two younger mechanics who have been "really good", he says, so there's at least some hope for the future.

He stresses again how rewarding he finds his work. The people for whom he fixes lifts tend to be very appreciative.

"I love that. You get that reaction from the customers," he says. "Without them, you got nothing."

articles.title: Argentina bars Central Bank from printing money to fund government spending
articles.summary: The South American country’s Senate also advances proposal to suspend primary elections ahead of 2027 presidential race.
articles.body:
Argentina’s legislature has pushed forward a series of bills that would implement changes sought by President Javier Milei , including barring the Central Bank from printing extra money for government expenses.

On Thursday, the Argentinian Chamber of Deputies gave final approval to a bill imposing restrictions on the Central Bank, defining its “primary and fundamental mission” as maintaining the value of the country’s currency.

Under past administrations, the Central Bank has printed additional funds to help cover government expenses, contributing to the country’s once sky-high inflation, which reached more than 200 percent in 2023.

Milei, a libertarian economist, swept into office that year on a promise to tame runaway inflation and slash government spending.

Under his leadership, inflation has declined, though poverty has surged. Economists also believe Argentina may be drifting into a recession, with economic activity diminished in recent months.

Still, Milei’s office celebrated the Senate’s passage of the Central Bank bill with a presidential statement.

“This marks the end of nearly two decades of political manipulation at the Central Bank,” the statement said.

The bank, founded in 1935, had experienced “91 years of plunder, expropriation, impunity, and institutional decay” up to this point, it added.

The vote in the Chamber of Deputies was 141 to zero, with 99 abstentions.

The Senate previously passed the bill, though it removed language Milei had pressed for, which would have required a two-thirds vote in both chambers of Congress to remove Central Bank governors.

Also on Thursday, Argentina’s Senate advanced a bill to reform the country’s elections by suspending its primaries.

Unlike the Central Bank reform, that bill was not final. It still needs to pass the Chamber of Deputies.

The bill, however, comes less than a year before Argentina is slated to hold its next presidential election. Milei is expected to seek re-election in the October 24 vote.

Critics see the suspension of primaries as a means for Milei to avoid early pushback in his campaign.

A dismal primary result, they say, could weaken his momentum ahead of the general election and cause unfavourable economic fluctuations. Milei has long faced public discontent over his programme of economic austerity .

Thursday’s bill would also reduce public financing for political parties and eliminate a mandatory presidential debate ahead of general elections.

Senators approved the legislation by a vote of 43 to 29. While members of Milei’s La Libertad Avanza party touted the bill as a means of simplifying Argentina’s elections, opponents warned it could erode democratic norms.

“Milei now wants to change the rules of democracy to improve his chances of reelection by cheating,” Buenos Aires province Governor Axel Kicillof, a potential challenger to Milei, said in a social media post.

articles.title: Sheikh Hasina: Why her planned return from India has Bangladesh on edge
articles.summary: The ousted prime minister's December homecoming plan deepens Dhaka-Delhi tensions and risks fresh unrest.
articles.body:
Sheikh Hasina has repeatedly vowed to return to Bangladesh.

Now the ousted prime minister has put a date on her homecoming - 16 December - and even outlined how she intends to make the journey.

The government in Dhaka, which had previously dismissed the prospect, is taking her latest declaration more seriously.

Hasina, 79, who fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule, plans to go back on Victory Day, the anniversary of Bangladesh's triumph over Pakistan in the 1971 liberation war, her spokesperson said.

She was sentenced to death after being convicted of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown, in a trial held in her absence that raised questions about due process. Her Awami League party is banned in Bangladesh. The UN says as many as 1,400 people were killed by security forces during the uprising.

The government says she would be arrested immediately if she returned and has promised to carry out the death sentence.

Hasina now wants the Bangladesh government to arrange a flight from Delhi. If that fails, she could travel commercially or cross the land border.

"She is even prepared to walk into Bangladesh," Abu Obaidha Arin, a key aide to Hasina, told the BBC.

India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545 mile) border across five Indian states - West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Her supporters, Arin said, had identified nine possible crossing points. "This is a carefully thought-out, precise plan. This is serious."

Dhaka has responded with defiance, insisting Hasina must be extradited.

"Reality and desire are different things," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters in Dhaka. "[The reality is] she's not a regular commercial passenger. She can only be brought back in handcuffs."

India's foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Hasina's extradition request was being examined through the "established process", adding that a voluntary return would be a separate matter.

Many in Dhaka believe Hasina's declaration is more than a promise of homecoming.

They believe it is an attempt to test the government's authority, force her way back into the political conversation and exploit divisions among the parties that united to oust her. It also threatens to turn India's unresolved problem of sheltering a former ally into a more immediate diplomatic crisis.

The date is significant. Hasina is invoking Victory Day to reclaim her place in Bangladesh's founding narrative. Aides say she has spent months trying to keep her party alive in exile.

Arin says Hasina has been in regular contact with party leaders and workers through interactive audio conversations on Telegram, keeping alive a network that might otherwise have been difficult to sustain from exile.

Over the past 18 months, he says, she has held more than 300 such meetings, reaching supporters across all 64 districts and the country's 300 constituencies. They are organised through the Awami League's 78 units and "can last four or five hours".

The meetings allow Hasina to listen directly to party workers, hear their grievances and understand what is happening on the ground, Arin says. He insists the response has been substantial and claims the party "could mobilise five million people to welcome her along the route from the border to Dhaka, forming a human chain".

"We have the organisational capacity to make that happen," he says.

That may be an ambitious claim. The Awami League remains a mass party with millions of supporters, but it is banned and largely shut out of mainstream politics. Much of its leadership is abroad, in jail or underground. Police have arrested supporters and filed thousands of cases against party workers.

Yet its supporters have continued to take to the streets, staging flash protests that have grown more frequent and confrontational in recent months.

Several districts have reported bomb attacks, arson and vandalism, though responsibility for some incidents remains disputed.

Gopalganj, Hasina's ancestral district, has proved particularly difficult for the authorities to control.

Awami League supporters have attacked police stations , torched vehicles and targeted homes and offices belonging to ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leaders, reports say. Highways have been blocked with felled trees and burning tyres, bringing traffic to a standstill. In some areas, police have withdrawn amid fears of further attacks.

Supporters have staged 40 demonstrations and more than 140 riots up to 23 November, according to data from conflict monitoring group Acled (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project). At least 11 people, including two civilians, have been killed in political violence this month, six directly linked to the unrest, the group says.

The party's ability to cause disruption, however, is not necessarily evidence of a broad resurgence.

Many in Dhaka remain sceptical that Hasina will actually return, viewing the announcement as a means of galvanising a demoralised party.

Yet the Awami League has achieved something politically: it is back in the conversation. Immediately after Hasina's fall, even mentioning the party was taboo. Now its future is being debated across the political spectrum.

Shafiqul Alam, editor of the English-language daily Daily Waadaa and former press secretary to the Muhammad Yunus-led interim government, believes the party is "exploiting cracks in the unity forged during the uprising".

He told the BBC that "disagreements" over the July Charter , proposed constitutional changes and the referendum have "widened divisions" between the elected BNP government and rivals Jamaat-e-Islami and the youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP).

"The Awami League sees an opening," Alam told the BBC. "The party believes this is an opportune moment to take to the streets, exploiting a weakened police force and divisions among the forces of the July uprising ."

Analysts say if Hasina returns it could just as easily deepen hostility as revive her party's fortunes. The government has framed the sporadic recent violence as terrorism, while supporters insist their demonstrations are peaceful and accuse the authorities of repression.

The larger question is whether Bangladesh can sustain the exclusion of a political constituency as substantial as the Awami League without creating another source of instability.

For India, the dilemma is increasingly difficult to manage.

Delhi has sheltered Hasina, but her public remarks have angered Dhaka, which wants her extradited. India has sought to repair ties through diplomatic outreach and talks on trade, border security and other bilateral issues, but relations remain strained.

The chill is striking: nearly 10 months into his tenure, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India.

A trip was reportedly in the offing in August, but Hasina's press conference in Delhi proved a setback to efforts to reset relations.

Avinash Paliwal, who teaches politics and international studies at SOAS University of London, argues that Hasina's latest announcement has "shifted the burden of choice to Dhaka rather than Delhi".

Delhi, he says, "feels it has tried its best" to work with Rahman's government over the past 10 months - "from appointing a political heavyweight as high commissioner with cabinet rank to offering fresh talks on security and trade".

"The failure of this outreach has left India disillusioned with Dhaka. India seems to have decided that bilateral relations will likely remain tense whatever it does, so there is little reason to stop Hasina from stirring the political pot."

Delhi has the leverage to restrain Hasina from making political statements on Indian soil, Paliwal argues, but may not want to exercise it.

Nor, in his view, is it in India's interest to see the Awami League permanently excluded from Bangladeshi politics.

"The political party still enjoys pockets of support across Bangladesh and is weaved into the social and political fabric of the country," he says. "So, yes, it is in India's interest, and also in Bangladesh's long-term interests, to rehabilitate the Awami League and take the path of political reconciliation."

That view is increasingly contested in Dhaka.

"There is a perception in Bangladesh that India wants to rehabilitate the Awami League. There are issues India has not resolved, including the extradition of Hasina. India has also not renewed the transit facilities that could benefit Bangladeshi garment exporters, while the Ganges water treaty is nearing expiry without much progress. But has India done enough to win back trust?" says Alam.

"For now, only tourist and medical visas have resumed. Everything else remains in limbo."

A Dhaka-based foreign-policy expert, who asked not to be named, says the two countries remain locked in "mutual frustration".

Hasina, he says, remains central to the impasse. "She remains the elephant in the room, but we also have to find a way to move beyond Hasina."

Paliwal argues that the least damaging outcome for India would be Hasina returning to face a fresh trial, with the Awami League rehabilitated under a different operational leadership.

"It will reintroduce a degree of balance in Bangladeshi politics, and will afford India space to protect its long-term interests and equities better," he says.

For now, 16 December is not yet a confirmed journey. But Hasina has already succeeded in making her return a question that neither Dhaka nor Delhi can ignore.

"December could be chaotic. Everyone in Dhaka is on edge," says the foreign-policy expert, warning of protests and confrontation as Hasina's proposed return date approaches - and the possibility that it could be postponed yet again.

"Hasina is unlikely to return, as she would face a death sentence. But her comments have clearly galvanized her supporters," says Pearl Pandya, Acled's South Asia analyst.

But the impasse is also complicating India's ties with Bangladesh. As Paliwal puts it, the "next window of serious negotiations will now open only after Hasina returns to Dhaka, or Dhaka relents under pressure and returns to the table".

articles.title: Inside the rogue trader networks scamming customers at scale
articles.summary: Networks of plumbers and electricians are scamming people on a large scale, the BBC reveals.
articles.body:
Organised networks of rogue plumbers and electricians have been scamming people on a large scale, a BBC investigation has found.

Nessar Khawaja, who used the online name ThatGuyNess, regularly posted TikTok videos showing his work as a plumber, explaining how he made thousands of pounds from "desperate" customers, and recruiting online to expand his network.

"Me and my team, we're top of the food chain," he said in one video.

The investigation found the 23-year-old is a key figure within an organised group that is systematically ripping off customers and teaching others to do the same.

The BBC put these allegations to Khawaja in writing. He denied any wrongdoing and said his social media posts were intended as light-hearted comedy that did not reflect how he operated in practice.

In a recorded phone call, Khawaja insisted he was an entertainer, was joking and that the BBC had "taken things out of context".

In another video, Khawaja made claims he had electricians working for him who made more than £40,000 a month.

"I've got 100-120 engineers. Imagine how much money I am making them and making from them," he said.

One of Khawaja's associates told an undercover BBC journalist during a secretly-recorded recruitment call that engineers working for them had to hand over 60% from every job to the network.

After being approached for comment, TikTok said it banned the account for "breaching its rules on fraud and scams".

Trading Standards said the average rogue trader call-out scam now costs the victim about £10,000.

Clive, who lives in London, is undergoing treatment for cancer.

He said he had felt forced to pay the rogue trader who came to his home and charged £9,153 for installing an outdoor socket to fit garden lights he already owned.

An independent electrical expert told the BBC the job had not been done properly, was left in an unsafe state and should have cost no more than £250.

Clive said he no longer feels safe in his home.

He explained how he had searched for a local electrician on Google when his usual tradesperson was unavailable and came across Chriss Electrician Ltd.

Clive said the engineer spent about two hours at the property before presenting him with the bill.

He added he had felt pressured into paying as the work had already been completed.

He went to his local bank branch to move money between accounts before returning home and making the payment through the engineer's portable card reader.

Despite his doubts about the costs, Clive said he had feared what might happen if he refused to pay.

"If I hadn't paid him, I thought something might happen," he said.

"When people come to the door now, I think, 'Oh God, who's that?' I don't feel safe any more."

While the BBC has not seen evidence that Khawaja controls or runs this company, it has established the following:

Companies House places Chriss Electrician Ltd at an address in Ilford

Khawaja appears as the listed director of two dissolved companies inside that same building, one inside the very same flat

Khawaja's company First Choice Maintenance 24/7 Limited was registered 22 days before Chriss Electrician Ltd was incorporated and registered at the same flat as its address.

The BBC contacted Chriss Electrician Ltd for comment but it has not responded.

Khawaja denied having any connection with Chriss Electrician Ltd.

Clive was refunded by his bank after it was contacted by the BBC. The bank said it had done so as a "gesture of goodwill".

'I was threatened with rape after locksmith scam'

Secret filming catches locksmith charging 10 times quote

Like Clive, another man, who the BBC has named as Tom, felt he had no choice but to settle the bill when he mistakenly called a rogue trader to his property in Essex after finding a leak.

He says he was initially quoted £49 over the phone after calling a listing at the top of Google purporting to be an established business.

But on arrival, the plumber increased the call-out fee to £250 and the costs kept on climbing.

"He charged us for the first load of repairs, and then the second load with the water cylinder. Basically, he was running my taps constantly saying, 'Look, it's coming out this hot', which caused me to panic."

By the end, the plumber presented a bill for £6,237.60.

"I noticed afterwards that the invoice said Ibby & Co. Ltd. That was when alarm bells started ringing because I had never heard of that company. It wasn't the company I called out, essentially."

Tom called another plumber to get a second opinion and was told the work that was completed should have cost no more than £1,000.

When Tom called the company to complain, he received threats from an unknown man. The call was recorded and the BBC heard threats including: "We'll show up at your house. And we're gonna be sleeping there for months."

Ibrahim Nazir, the plumber who came to Tom's property and the listed director of Ibby and Co Ltd, has been contacted by the BBC for comment but has not responded.

Sources close to Khawaja place Nazir inside the same network.

Khawaja said he did not know anything about the job involving Tom and stated Nazir was not in his employ.

Monetising vulnerability and desperation is key to the rogue trader business model, insiders say.

One insider forwarded the BBC a script being circulated by a different rogue trader network recruiting young men for commission-based work.

The document tells recruits to hike prices if children or pets are trapped inside and even instructs them to fake picking a lock for seven minutes before drilling it.

Lee, not his real name, spent a year working for Khawaja as a plumber until, he says, his conscience got the better of him.

"It got a bit too much for me," he said. "I didn't like scamming people. So, I left.

"I've worked for London's biggest plumbing company and, no word of a lie, this lot have more jobs. They're giants."

Rather than relying on solid reputations and recommendation, rogue traders rely on search engine traffic.

They either pay to get their details at the top of Google, which means they are seen first, or they mimic the names of reputable companies by making tiny changes to the business name.

Reached by the BBC's undercover journalist posing as a plumber seeking to work with them, one of Khawaja's associates said: "We're a lead company. We'll send you jobs, and then you go to the jobs.

"We sort the jobs through online advertisement. Usually we'll try and get emergencies so we can charge more. You make up the pricing."

The associate told the undercover reporter they had to charge in the region of £400 for every job, regardless of what work was actually needed.

Both Clive and Tom reported what happened to the Metropolitan Police and Essex Police.

Khawaja said he was not a party to the phone call with the undercover journalist and could not comment on its contents.

He said the alleged statements did not reflect how he operates.

He separately told the BBC in the recorded phone call: "You guys should know I am an entertainer and you guys are taking it out of context."

"I am clearly joking and I'm entertaining and I am engaging with the comments, it is not literal," he added.

He said the right of reply sent to him by the BBC contained "false information which has nothing to do with me".

TikTok said its community guidelines were "clear" and did not "allow any attempts to scam, trick or defraud people".

The firm said in the three months up to June 2026, it had removed 99.2% of content found to be in breach of its "policies on fraud and scams... before it was reported to us".

The BBC put questions to Google including why rogue traders were able to advertise on its platform. It did not answer specific questions, but a Google spokesperson said: "We have strict ads policies that govern the types of ads and advertisers we allow on our platforms.

"Keeping our users and partners safe is our top priority and we invest heavily in the enforcement of our policies.

"We have a team of thousands working around the clock to create and enforce our policies at scale."

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: 'Scores' of Labour MPs oppose Rosebank and 'Shameless Huw'
articles.summary: Labour MPs oppose Rosebank oilfield and 'Shameless Huw'
articles.body:
The Guardian reports that Labour's internal divisions over the Rosebank oil field have "spilled into the open" , after nearly 100 MPs signed a letter opposing the project. One frontbencher - who is said to be considering resigning - tells the Times that, for some MPs, tackling climate change is their "number one reason for being Labour". But a colleague supportive of the project is quoted as saying that "the anti-crowd are resorting to internal party politics".

The "participation fee" the UK has to pay to the EU as part of the post-Brexit reset deal is described in the Financial Times as a "pay-to-play" charge . The details of the deal also include what the paper calls a "Farage clause", which EU diplomats say is aimed at deterring Reform or the Conservatives from "ripping up" the agreement.

The governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, tells the Times that banks are likely to pass on the cost of higher taxes to customers. Last month, the Chancellor John Healey used his first Budget to hike levies on banks. But the paper says they could respond by offering more expensive loans or less generous interest rates on deposits.

articles.title: New Zealand election results: Ruling coalition loses parliamentary majority
articles.summary: The right-leaning ruling bloc led by the National Party has fallen short of the majority needed to govern.
articles.body:
New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.

It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.

The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.

A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.

Luxon on Friday acknowledged that negotiations "may be challenging" and will take some time.

"Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls," he told reporters.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said his party "ran an incredible campaign" but acknowledged that it doesn't have negotiating power despite winning the popular vote. "More New Zealanders voted for change at this election than for the status quo," he said.

New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each person casts two votes – one for their preferred political party and another for their choice of local representative.

Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, picked up five.

Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. Opportunity's leader Qiulae Wong told reporters her party will negotiate with National, but that all options remain on the table.

"There are seven parties in parliment and everyone is responsible for making sure we do everything we can to deliver a stable government for New Zealand. It's not just up to us," she said on Friday.

Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc.

But today's official tally shows it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left.

Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence.

Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things.

In earlier interviews with the BBC, many voters had expressed frustration over spiralling costs of living and high unemployment across the country, with declining faith in their political leadership.

"There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread," said 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger.

A 40-year-old man said he didn't vote as he could not bring himself to tick any of the boxes on the ballot paper.

More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the Helen Clark Foundation, a public policy think tank.

Kiwis have been leaving the country in record numbers, with many of them, including former prime minister Jacinda Arden , moving to Australia.

articles.title: Kolkata man buys 2 plates of chicken momos for Rs 109 each, is charged Rs 10 extra for takeaway packaging; consumer commission orders outlet to refund  fee, pay Rs 100 compensation, Rs 2,000 legal costs and deposit Rs 50,000 in legal aid fund
articles.summary: KOLKATA: A Kolkata food outlet has been asked to pay Rs 50,000 to a consumer commission's legal aid fund for charging a customer Rs 10 to pack two plates
articles.body: KOLKATA: A Kolkata food outlet has been asked to pay Rs 50,000 to a consumer commission's legal aid fund for charging a customer Rs 10 to pack two plates of chicken momos, with the commission ruling that takeaway packaging is the seller's responsibility. The customer had bought two plates of chicken momos, each priced at Rs 109, from the outlet on October 29, 2024. The additional Rs 10 on the bill for packaging led to a dispute after the customer sought a refund of the amount, which the outlet declined to provide.The customer then approached the consumer commission, seeking relief over the charge. In its defence, the company claimed the customer had asked for extra packaging because he was travelling on a motorcycle and wanted to avoid spillage while keeping the food safe and hygienic. It said the fee had been disclosed in advance and that the customer had accepted it before placing the order.The commission, however, found no material on record to support the company's version. It said the outlet could not establish either that the customer had requested the packaging or that he had been told about the additional charge beforehand. The bench of president Manoj Kumar Rai and member Gopal Chandra Roy relied on Section 36(5) of the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, which places the cost of making goods fit for delivery on the seller, unless there is an agreement to the contrary. The commission said the outlet was therefore required to pack the food for takeaway at its own expense. Charging the customer for this service, without proving that he had specifically sought it or agreed to pay for it, amounted to deficiency in service.The outlet has been directed to return the Rs 10 packaging fee and pay Rs 100 as compensation to the customer, besides Rs 2,000 towards litigation costs. articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Thursday said President Vladimir Putin would be welcome to attend the G20 summit in Florida next month if he wanted to, although he doubted the Russian leader would make the trip."If he wanted to come, he certainly can," Trump told reporters at his Florida golf resort, where he was celebrating Thanksgiving.He said some people would not like to see Putin at the December 14-15 summit, but added, "If it were up to me, I'd like to have him."The Kremlin said on Thursday that no decision had been taken on Putin's participation in the summit.The Russian president had said after meeting Trump last week that he would consider attending after discussing it with the US leader, but would also take the situation in Russia into account, Reuters reported.Trump further recalled Russia's earlier membership in the Group of Eight (G8), saying former US president Barack Obama had wanted Moscow removed from the grouping and that Putin had been "very insulted" by the decision."When he was a member of the G8, if he stayed a member--President Obama wanted him out, and if he stayed a member, you might not have this war right now. He was very insulted when that happened. And now it's the G7, and to be honest with you, all we do is talk about Russia. I said, 'Why isn't he here?'" Trump said."I believe if they didn't do that, I really believe strongly that if they didn't do that, we would not have that war going on right now. The First Lady wouldn't have to go over and try to get a ceasefire to get people out. Some of the people are very old people, and get people out," he added.Trump also said Putin wanted to reach an agreement to end the Russia-Ukraine war, arguing that maintaining a cordial relationship with the Russian leader was important to negotiations.Speaking during a Thanksgiving call with US military personnel alongside First Lady Melania Trump from his Mar-a-Lago residence, Trump said his priority was to stop the ongoing loss of lives."Well, things can be said, but look, you have to understand something. We want to make a deal. We want to stop killing," he said."I could say he's not a friend or with it, well, I want to make a deal. I got to get a deal done. They're losing 25,000 people a month," he added.Trump said openly expressing hostility towards Putin could complicate efforts to reach a settlement, drawing a comparison with the strained relationship between the Russian leader and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy."I could walk in and say, 'I don't like you,' and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelenskyy and Putin. You know, they have the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other, okay?" Trump said.He also referred to investigations into alleged Russian interference in US politics, which he called a "fake" investigation, before reiterating that his recent discussion with Putin had been positive."So when I go and happen to get along with him--I've known him a long time, don't forget he had to suffer through a fake 'Russia, Russia, Russia' investigation, which was made up and totally-- was a total con job. And he had to go through that and hear things that turned out to be totally false. So, we had a very good discussion. The bottom line is he would like to make a deal," Trump said.In a separate post on Truth Social, Trump said he had urged Putin during their recent discussions in China to withdraw military aggression across Europe to facilitate a quick agreement between Russia and Ukraine."During my conversations in China with President Vladimir Putin of Russia, I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe, in the hopes that a Deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine, and made quickly," Trump wrote."I really believe this is a strong possibility. Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH, and will be a Great Tribute to everyone!" he added.Trump's remarks followed his meeting with Nato secretary general Mark Rutte at Mar-a-Lago.According to a joint statement issued after the meeting, the two leaders discussed the Russia-Ukraine war and the conflict in Iran, including the need for Russia to avoid actions that could widen the conflict and the urgency of securing a peaceful settlement.You use AI every day. articles.summary: TSAA trainer Cessna crash-lands at Golconda Cantonment after engine failure; trainee pilot and instructor suffer minor injuries as DGCA probes incident.
articles.body: HYDERABAD: A trainer aircraft of the Telangana State Aviation Academy (TSAA) suffered an engine failure mid-air and crash-landed at the Golconda Cantonment parade grounds on Thursday afternoon. The trainee pilot and her instructor escaped with minor injuries.The two-seater Cessna, which had taken off from Begumpet airport on a training sortie, was flying at around 3,000 feet when its engine failed. The trainee and instructor managed to steer the aircraft towards an open stretch inside Golconda Cantonment and attempted a forced landing. The aircraft, however, struck a tree while coming down and was damaged.“After observing the engine had failed, the pilots decided to force-land it. On seeing the plain location at parade grounds inside the Golconda Cantonment, they decided to land the aircraft there. They almost successfully did, but the aircraft came in touch with a tree leading to the accident,’’ an official from the academy said.The accident occurred around 1pm, nearly two hours after the aircraft had taken off from Begumpet airport for the training exercise.Military personnel rushed to the damaged aircraft and helped bring the two occupants out. They were later shifted to a private hospital.A senior Hyderabad police officer told TOI that both were safe and being treated for minor injuries.An academy official said this was the first accident in the last 20 years involving a TSAA trainer aircraft.The unusual sight of a light aircraft coming down inside the Cantonment drew the attention of civilians in the vicinity, with many rushing towards the area to find out what had happened.Asked if the incident had triggered panic inside the Cantonment, an official said: “It was not a military aircraft. They also understood that it was a training aircraft.’’DCP (Golconda zone) J Raghavendra Reddy told TOI that a case will be registered and a letter will be sent to officials of the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) to conduct a probe on the cause of the accident.“Officials of the DGCA came to the spot and took stock,” he said.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Hyderabad | Silver Rate in Hyderabad | Bank Holidays in Hyderabad | Public Holidays in Hyderabad | Hyderabad AQI | Weather in Hyderabad | Petrol Price in Hyderabad | Diesel Price in Hyderabad | CNG Price in Hyderabad | LPG Price in HyderabadStay updated with the latest Hyderabad news. articles.title: Tamil Nadu rain alert: IMD warns of heavy rain in Theni Ghat areas, thunderstorms across state till Saturday as northeast monsoon revives after weeks of deficit
articles.summary: CHENNAI: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast heavy rain in the Ghat areas of Theni district on Friday, while thunderstorms accompanied
articles.body: CHENNAI: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast heavy rain in the Ghat areas of Theni district on Friday, while thunderstorms accompanied by lightning and gusty winds are likely to continue across Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal until Saturday.The warning comes as the northeast monsoon regained strength over southern Tamil Nadu on Thursday after weeks of inadequate rainfall, bringing heavy showers to coastal districts, flooding roads and school premises and forcing restrictions at popular waterfalls.Kayalpattinam in Thoothukudi district recorded 18cm of rain in the 24 hours ending Thursday morning. Following overnight showers that inundated school premises, district collector Vishu Mahajan declared a holiday for schools in Tiruchendur taluk on Thursday.Waterlogging was reported near Mutharamman temple, the police station and arterial roads in Kulasekarapattinam, inconveniencing motorists and devotees. Udangudi, Manapad and several other coastal villages also received heavy rainfall.In Tirunelveli, intermittent showers continued into Thursday evening. Heavy rain in the Western Ghats triggered a rise in water levels near Manimuthar, prompting authorities to restrict tourist access. In neighbouring Tenkasi, bathing at Courtallam Main Falls was prohibited following a sharp increase in water flow.The restriction disappointed Sabarimala pilgrims who traditionally stop at the falls to bathe on their way to Kerala. However, tourists were allowed to bathe at Five Falls, Old Courtallam and some smaller waterfalls on Thursday morning.Reservoirs receive fresh inflowsThe rainfall brought some relief to reservoirs across southern Tamil Nadu, with Papanasam and Manimuthar dams receiving more water than they released. Pechiparai and Perunchani reservoirs in Kanyakumari district also recorded fresh inflows.However, water storage in several major reservoirs remained considerably below last year's levels. Storage in Mullaperiyar and Vaigai continued to decline, with Vaigai holding only 39% of its capacity.The showers are significant for the region, where Madurai and Theni had recorded seasonal rainfall deficits of 34% and 23%, respectively, until Tuesday. The shortfall has raised concerns over water availability for irrigation and drinking purposes.Chennai unlikely to get significant rainWhile southern and western Tamil Nadu are expected to receive further showers, Chennai and neighbouring districts may see only isolated light rainfall spells for the remainder of November.V R Durai, director of the Area Cyclone Warning Centre at the Regional Meteorological Centre (RMC), Chennai, said the easterly trough that was expected to bring rainfall to Tamil Nadu had shifted westwards, taking rain-bearing activity towards Kerala.“There is no possibility for rainfall over north TN, including Chennai, at least till the end of Nov,” he said.According to the IMD forecast, heavy rain is likely at isolated places in the Ghat areas of Theni on Friday (November 27). Thunderstorms accompanied by lightning and gusty winds of 30-40kmph are likely at one or two places across Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal until Saturday (November 28).On November 28, moderate rain is likely over the delta, southern and western districts, while isolated light showers may occur elsewhere. North Tamil Nadu and some delta and central districts may remain largely dry on November 29.Light rain is forecast at isolated places over north coastal Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal on November 30. Moderate showers are likely over coastal Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal on December 1, while southern and delta districts are expected to receive moderate rain on December 2. Light rain may occur over the remaining parts of Tamil Nadu and Puducherry.Durai said a low-pressure area was also likely to form over the south Andaman Sea, but its eventual movement remained uncertain. Forecast models could change as the system develops, he added.Chennai is likely to record a maximum temperature of 31-32°C and a minimum of 24-25°C on Friday.Tamil Nadu has so far recorded a 15% deficit in northeast monsoon rainfall. articles.title: At least 13 Niger soldiers killed in Sanam armed attack
articles.summary: It remains unclear who carried out the attack on Niger’s National Guard in Tillaberi, near the Mali border.
articles.body:
At least 13 members of Niger’s National Guard have been killed and 20 wounded in an attack on their compound in Sanam, in the west of the country, the Defence Ministry has said.

In a statement read on state television, the ministry said the attack on Thursday was carried out by “numerous heavily armed assailants”, referring to the incident as a “terrorist attack”.

The ministry gave a provisional toll and said soldiers killed several attackers and destroyed their logistical infrastructure. Operations to track down the attackers are ongoing, it added.

The assault took place at about 5am local time (04:00 GMT), local and security sources told the Nigerien outlet ActuNiger.

Sanam is in the Tillaberi region, near the Mali border, where armed groups regularly attack security forces.

It was not clear who was behind the attack.

The attack comes two days after the ministry said 11 soldiers were killed in an attack attributed to Boko Haram in the Diffa region, in the southeast.

In neighbouring Nigeria, suspected members of an armed group killed at least 30 people in villages in the central state of Niger on Tuesday.

They described it as retaliation for the killing of many Fulani herders days earlier.

In Nigeria’s northeast, President Bola Tinubu promised on Wednesday to restore peace to a region hit by a rebellion led by Boko Haram and the ISIL (ISIS) affiliate in West Africa Province, as he campaigns for re-election.
