articles.title: Israel uses south Lebanon Christian villages to try to divide and conquer
articles.summary: Israel is trying to fragment Lebanon by separating its Christian residents in south Lebanon from the rest.
articles.body:
Beirut, Lebanon – On Lebanon’s Independence Day on Sunday, Israel’s Arabic-language military spokesperson Ella Waweya posted a video on X in a classroom in Dibil, a Christian village in south Lebanon.

In the video, she wished Lebanese a happy national day, praised the singer Fairuz, and blamed the Lebanese armed group Hezbollah, which is fighting an ongoing war against Israel, for the hardships faced by the people in southern Lebanon.

The video drew widespread condemnation from Lebanese officials, including from Dibil’s municipality, who told local media that the visit took place around a month before the video was posted.

The council said the visit took place “without prior coordination with the school administration”. The Israeli military said an investigation was reviewing the incident and it is not clear whether Waweya had official approval to post the video.

Unlike neighbouring Shia Muslim villages, Christian villages in southern Lebanon have generally been allowed to stay on their lands during Israel’s war on Lebanon. But they still live under Israeli occupation.

“We’re in a giant prison,” Ayoub Khreish, the president of Ain Ebl municipality, told Al Jazeera from his village on Lebanon’s southern border. “We can only move around in these [neighbouring] villages. Anytime we want to go to Beirut, we need to get permission.”

This system goes through a so-called “mechanism”, whereby a request is submitted to the Lebanese Army, which passes it to the UN and then onto the Israelis for approval.

Now living under the Israeli military’s authority, these Christian villages are being used as part of an Israeli strategy to foment divides among the Lebanese population, experts told Al Jazeera.

Israel launched a massive assault on Lebanon in October 2023, shortly after genocide in Gaza began, with approximately 9,000 people killed since then, according to Lebanon’s Ministry of Public Health.

Southern Lebanon, where Hezbollah has a presence, has been the area worst affected by the violence, with thousands of Israeli air raids and repeated Israeli raids in villages.

Israel’s war on Lebanon has left Christians in southern villages in a precarious position. Much of the south has been made uninhabitable by Israeli attacks and demolitions. While Shia Muslims have taken the overwhelming brunt of the violence, Christians have been killed in attacks and been displaced, too.

In early November, the mayors of five Christian villages appealed to the Council of Catholic Patriarchs and Bishops of Lebanon, asking for help so residents can remain on their land and displaced people can return.

“Help us make staying on our land a choice of life based on security, dignity, work and hope, rather than an anxious wait in uncertainty,” they wrote at the time.

Khreish, municipal president of Ain Ebl, said a little more than half of the town’s population fled since the start of the war. Daily convoys bring in food and other necessities, but the local economy has ground to a halt.

He initially hoped for a political solution to the crisis, but a June framework agreement between Israel and Lebanon that looked to have Israeli troops withdraw from the south and Hezbollah disarm has not progressed as originally hoped. Talks between the two sides have been stalled since August.

“We thought peace and a political solution would be closer than this,” he said. “But the opposite seems to be true; it’s far off.”

As the occupation drags on, Lebanese in these villages feel they are forced to deal with the political reality in front of them. Khreish said Israeli soldiers enter the village regularly and interact with locals.

“We’re no longer afraid of them,” Khreish said. “We’re under their authority, the authority of the Israeli military.”

Experts say this particular treatment of Christians in Lebanon is part of a wider strategy to fragment and divide the local population.

“It’s part of a longstanding strategy on behalf of Israel towards the minorities of the region to divide and conquer,” Munira Khayyat, author of Landscape of War: Ecologies of Resistance and Survival in South Lebanon, told Al Jazeera. “You see this happening, of course, in Palestine, and in Lebanon, they’ve always done this. They always had this strategy of separating the Christians from their social, ethnic, national and historical environment to reinvent them as foot soldiers for the Zionist cause.”

In July, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who may soon be out of office, claimed that Lebanon’s Christians were asking Israel for protection from its Muslim neighbours.

“Christian villages in Lebanon, some of them have actually asked to be annexed to Israel, because we protect them against Hezbollah, Hezbollah fanatics who want to kill them, and we do the same things with Christians everywhere,” Netanyahu told Fox News.

Netanyahu’s claims were rejected by Lebanese officials, including Hanna al-Amil, president of the Rmeish Municipality, the largest Christian-majority border village.

A statement was signed by 15 villages in southern Lebanon that called the claim “completely fabricated” and “unrelated to reality”.

Michael Young, a Lebanese political analyst and writer at the Beirut-based Carnegie Center, said Israel aimed to show the outside world, and the US in particular, that it protects Christians and other minorities after its actions in Gaza turned public opinion heavily against it. In Gaza, Israel had bombed Christian churches , where many Palestinians sought refuge from the Israeli genocide.

“People like [US political commentator] Tucker Carlson are playing this up, so from a public relations perspective, they want to show they are friendly to all minorities; Druze, Christians and so on,” Young said.

Experts said that the Israeli efforts to cater to minorities in the region are more than an external public relations campaign.

“There is another much more sinister reason,” Young said. “The Israelis have a policy in the region of fragmentation.”

Young pointed to a paper ( PDF ) published in October by Tamir Hayman, a former chief of the Israeli military’s Intelligence Directorate and the current executive director of the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), an Israeli think tank.

In the paper, Hayman outlines what he discerns as Israel’s new, unwritten national security concepts. One key concept is the Israeli national security view that “Arab states are not genuine nation-states, but collections of tribes and ethnic groups lacking a shared history and a foundational national vision.”

“Consequently, undermining their stability is viewed as a natural process, one that Israel can manage more effectively than it can contend with strong nation-states, and one that it should even encourage,” Hayman continues.

In south Lebanon, locals of all denominations have expressed frustration or anger towards Hezbollah over the last few years.

“There is anger against Hezbollah, no doubt about it. But people criticising Hezbollah are not automatically with Israel,” said Young.

Many Lebanese Christians have been shocked by the destruction wrought on Shia villages around them and find it “inconceivable they can live without their Shia neighbours”.

Back in Ain Ebl, Khreish said the war and occupation had left them feeling stuck and that any effort to travel outside their area brings “constant anxiety”.

“We just hope for peace and that there won’t be war on us. What has this war brought us?” he said.

Like many others from south Lebanon, these Christian-predominant towns and villages feel they are stuck in limbo, waiting to see what comes next.

“We don’t think of the future. We live day by day. We don’t have eyes on the future because we don’t know what will happen,” Khreish said.

articles.title: Lowestoft will play huge role in UK future, says energy minister
articles.summary: Michael Shanks visits Lowestoft as it is confirmed as the main base for the new Vanguard windfarms.
articles.body:
Energy Minister Michael Shanks has said new windfarms which are about to be built off England's east coast will bring new jobs and economic opportunities to Lowestoft.

He said the Suffolk town that had been so important to Britain's past would once again play a "huge role" in the country's economic future.

The minister was speaking during a visit to the town's port to see preparatory work for the new Vanguard East and West windfarms.

The company says the project will support 3,000 jobs, of which the majority will be in the east of England.

Construction of the new windfarms is due to start in early 2027 after the energy company RWE secured £12bn of funding for the project, including £1bn from the UK government.

The Vanguard field which is 50 to 80km (about 31 to 49 miles) off the Norfolk coast will have 184 wind turbines and power three million homes.

The company says it will be one of the largest windfarms in the world and has confirmed that Lowestoft will be the main base for its construction and service operations.

The minister said the project was important for the country's energy security and to the government's aim to produce more clean power and reduce bills.

"But this should also be an opportunity for economic regeneration," he said

"Towns like Lowestoft which have been so important in our industrial past now have a hugely important role to play in our economic future [with] projects like Vanguard being built here with jobs that go with it and billions of pounds worth of investment."

RWE estimates that during the three-year construction phase, the projects will support more than 2,800 jobs directly and indirectly and another 300 once operational.

It says these will be high-skilled and well-paid with many of the jobs going to local people.

"It starts with mainly turbine technicians but then we'll have supply chain jobs on vessels and people running warehouses," said Tom Glover, the UK chair for RWE.

"Then it filters into the local economy: hotel jobs, sandwich jobs, taxi jobs."

The company is already offering work placements, sponsoring local college courses and recruiting apprentices.

Glover said that in Grimsby, where the company already has a large presence, 90% of staff whose work is associated with RWE live within a 20-mile radius.

Jack Eglington and Jersey Holmes, both 19 and from Lowestoft, are two of RWE's first apprentices.

Eglington is training to be a wind turbine technician and Holmes is a health and safety apprentice.

"To have these opportunities right here and be close to home and your family is so important for me," said Holmes.

"Most young people have to move away to find work but now that it's on my doorstep I can see myself staying around for a long time"

Eglington agreed, saying: "We're getting qualifications while we're learning how to do the job and there are so many progression opportunities if we want a whole career [here] we can.

"I get a great sense of pride that RWE are really invested in this area and in young people."

The two apprentices said the growth of offshore energy had already changed Lowestoft, which used to be a major fishing port.

"My grandparents tell me how the town used to be thriving with all the fishing, then they say it just dried up but now they can see it returning," said Eglington.

Holmes said: "There are more people about and there are more people coming here for work. It is benefitting hotels and restaurants – it's just great."

articles.title: Rock stars sign guitar to support Northumberland nature scheme
articles.summary: Sam Fender, Sting, Paul McCartney, Mark Knopfler and Joan Armatrading are supporting the project.
articles.body:
A guitar signed by Sir Paul McCartney, Sam Fender and Sting is set to be auctioned off to raise money for a nature restoration project.

The instrument, which has also has the autographs of Dire Straits star Mark Knopfler and Grammy Award nominee Joan Armatrading, is being sold to help fund work at the Rothbury Estate in Northumberland.

The Wildlife Trusts and Northumberland Wildlife Trust purchased the land after raising £30m to buy it from the son of the Duke of Northumberland, Lord Max Percy.

The Wildlife Trusts' head of major gifts, Debbie Johnson, said the north-east of England had a "rich musical heritage" and described the guitar as "very special".

"It has been wonderful to see many of the artists connected to the region and from beyond coming together to support a cause that means so much to the community," she said.

The trusts said they hoped music-lovers from around the world would be inspired to bid on the signed Fender Telecaster, which is being auctioned by Hanson Auctioneers on 9 December.

Auctioneer Charles Hanson said it was a "privilege" to be involved in the sale of a guitar" which had been "signed by some of the "greatest musicians ever known".

"To know that the proceeds will be going to such an important charity, responsible for some truly inspiring restoration projects, makes it even more important," he said.

The purchase of the 9,500 acre (3,845ha) estate was previously supported by Sir David Attenborough .

The land is home to a number of important species including red squirrels, cuckoos and curlews, and it is hoped work on the estate will allow them to thrive.

articles.title: Battle of bands brings Jersey and Guernsey footy rivalry to stage
articles.summary: The inaugural Music Muratti will see under-18 bands perform before industry judges.
articles.body:
Young musicians from Jersey and Guernsey will go head-to-head on Saturday in a new inter-island battle of the bands competition inspired by the Muratti football rivalry.

Music Muratti, launched by the School of Popular Music, will allow under-18 bands to represent their island in a contest at Beau Sejour Theatre in Guernsey.

Six bands, Fridge Magnet, Last Hope and Shockwave from Guernsey and Ctrl-3, Lupus and The Fadeaways from Jersey, will be lining up for the contest in front of music industry judges.

The winning bands will receive a professional studio recording and video session at their home island's School of Popular Music studio.

Autumn, guitarist for Jersey band Lupus, said the band initially entered the Music Muratti for fun but quickly realised it was a serious opportunity when they were selected.

She said: "When we actually got accepted, we were like, 'oh, this is real, guys.'"

The band described its sound as heavily influenced by 1990s rock, with Weezer among its biggest inspirations.

Autumn and fellow guitarist Keevan lead much of the songwriting and the group plans to perform an original track at the competition that is so new it does not yet have a title.

"I think us and the other Jersey bands are going to do really good against the Guernsey bands," she said.

School of Popular Music, a private school for musicians of all ages, was created by musician Tyler Edmonds in 2014, with bases in Jersey, Guersey and Dubai.

The annual Muratti Vase is an inter-island football match dating back to 1905 and is one of the highest-profile sporting events in the Channel Islands.

"The Muratti name means something to people here," said Edmonds.

"It stands for pride, for community, for two islands coming together and competing properly. We want Music Muratti to carry that same weight."

Every group is required to perform at least one original song and judges will choose the best Jersey band and the best Guernsey band, while one island will also be crowned overall Music Muratti champion.

The final is due to alternate between the islands each year, with Guernsey hosting the inaugural event and Jersey taking its turn in 2027.

articles.title: Harrow Council to set London's highest littering fines
articles.summary: Fines for littering will rise from £500 to £750 in Harrow, while fly-tipping will see a £5,000 penalty.
articles.body:
People caught littering or illegally dumping waste in a north-west London borough are set to face higher fines as the council steps up its efforts to tackle persistent fly-tipping.

Harrow Council has approved plans to increase penalties for littering, breaches of Public Space Protection Orders (PSPOs) and the most serious fly-tipping offences.

Penalties for littering will rise from £500 to £750, with a reduced penalty of £300 available for early payment - the highest to be introduced in the capital under a new national maximum cap.

The penalty for breaching a PSPO will increase from £100 to £500, while a new £5,000 penalty will be introduced for the most serious fly-tipping offences.

The changes follow an increase in the maximum penalties available to councils under government rules.

The highest fly-tipping penalty will only be used in cases involving "aggravating factors", such as hazardous waste or repeat offences.

Other factors include the dumping of multiple bags, whether the waste affects vulnerable people, and whether it was dumped by a business for financial gain.

Speaking at a cabinet meeting where the proposal was approved last week, councillor Pritesh Patel said: "The reason for these changes is that the government has increased the maximum penalties available to councils. This gives us an opportunity to strengthen our response to environmental crime.

"Most people do the right thing, but there is a minority that don't, and it is important that the consequences are meaningful and encourage prompt compliance and resolutions."

Harrow Council has tried a number of approaches to tackle fly-tipping over the years, including installing CCTV cameras in hotspots, sharing images and videos of offenders on social media and taking people to court.

But in January 2026, the council was criticised for failing to prosecute enough offenders at a fly-tipping hotspot in Harrow Weald.

Residents said a site on Weighton Road had to be cleared every few days. Despite a CCTV camera being in operation, only seven people had been sanctioned in the previous year.

One resident told a cabinet meeting in February that seven fines could be issued in a week, "let alone 52".

At the time, the council described the situation as "disgusting" following the long-running problems.

articles.title: Inside abandoned Devizes court as work starts to make it a museum
articles.summary: Work is starting to turn the abandoned Devizes Assize Court building into a museum.
articles.body:
The Assize Court in Devizes is a grand, listed building created in 1835 but abandoned with no other approved use for it until now.

Wiltshire Museum, currently at Long Street in the town, intends to relocate there and open it in 2030, but a lot of work needs to be done before that.

Stuart Henniker-Smith, from project managers, Chana Projects, said "at the moment, it's one big void in there".

"A lot of the existing original heritage fabric was missing or was in states of very serious disrepair," he added.

Staff also found evidence of squatters and a small fire when they first got in.

"For the first number of visits we were coming down here, it was all done by torch light. There's been no power in the building for a long, long time, so it's pitch black, so you're seeing snippets as you walk around with torches, trying to understand what it looks like, what's left, what it may look like," Henniker-Smith said.

He said it was in a "slightly worse condition" than they were hoping for in some places, but "it's not just a big empty box, it's an exciting building".

The plans include a extension at the back for a café below a gallery, accessibility and staircase at the side as well as renovating the building while preserving its heritage as much as possible.

Wiltshire Museum has world-renowned collection of gold found in the landscape around Stonehenge.

The building has been a much-loved feature of the town, with many wondering about its future.

Amber Pullen, from Wiltshire Museum, said it feels like a "load of mystery".

"If you like old derelict buildings, it's stunning. All the walls are full of just this wonderful story that it would be so wonderful to bring back to life.

"The cells are so captivating. There's so many stories, and I think that's what's also wonderful is through the archives, we've got a lot of stories that will tell the cells' stories and the people that have come through them."

She added that there are different types of cells and even tunnels to the courtrooms.

The museum will be using the space as galleries, but will also preserve the courts history and include it in any restoration.

Pullen, a Devizes local, grew up seeing the building and said she never understood why this was.

"I was obsessed with this building as a kid. I only went to school down the road I used to pass it every day and I loved it.

"When I finally saw that it was going to be the museum's new home, I think it just it makes sense doesn't it? It looks like a museum, so I think for me I can't wait."

The current work to make the building safer and enable the main work to begin will finish in January.

Specialist fitters will then create a museum space and carefully move artefacts, with the hope the public can be welcomed from 2030.

Wiltshire Museum is also currently signed up to the 'Big Give', which means any public donation during a certain amount of time is doubled.

articles.title: Western sanctions on Israeli settlers serve to shield the Israeli state
articles.summary: The settler takeover in Jericho exposes the inadequacy of sanctions targeting only settlers and their organisations.
articles.body:
On November 17, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman, Fadda Fheidat, was shot in the head and killed as she stood outside her home in al-Duyuk at-Tahta in Jericho. Fadda was murdered by Israeli settlers, who had recently forcibly evicted at least 13 Palestinian households from their homes in the neighbourhood.

What makes this takeover so significant is the location: the outskirts of Jericho, widely described as the world’s oldest continuously inhabited city and the first city to be handed over to the newly established Palestinian Authority in 1994 following the Oslo Accords.

Hours after Fadda was killed, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich visited the new settlement outpost and praised the settlers for what he characterised as a renewal of Jewish settlement in Jericho. It is the first Israeli settlement established inside a Palestinian city in the West Bank since settlers established a presence in the heart of Hebron nearly five decades ago.

This latest settler takeover was spearheaded by the far-right settler organisation Nachala with the support of the settler Binyamin Regional Council. Nachala was founded by the fanatical settler Daniella Weiss and has long campaigned for the ethnic cleansing and settlement of all of historic Palestine. Weiss and her organisation have gained international notoriety as a result of their relentless campaign calling for the Israeli government to complete the mass expulsion of Palestinians from Gaza and settle the area with Israelis.

Albeit politically significant, the takeover of homes in Jericho is not surprising. Since the genocide in Gaza began more than three years ago, Israeli settler takeover of Palestinian homes and land has drastically escalated in the West Bank. More than 6,000 Palestinians – half of whom are children – have been forcibly expelled as a result. The Israeli military has also been conducting its own expulsions. Between January and February 2025, the Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem refugee camps in the northern West Bank were emptied of their populations – some 33,000 residents.

One cannot separate the actions of the settlers and the military. The two work hand in glove towards their ultimate goal, which is to force as many Palestinians as possible off the land.

Both actors are part of a larger settler-colonial structure which enables this accelerating expansion. Indeed, the majority of settlements in the West Bank are connected to Israeli regime infrastructure, including Israeli-only roads and water and electricity networks, and many offer state subsidies as incentives for Jewish Israelis to live there. When one sees the settlements with one’s own eyes, it is clear that there is no separation between them and the Israeli state.

Yet the distinction between settlers and the settler-colonial structure is a useful tool for Israel’s more liberal supporters. To blame the settlers and a few more extreme ministers is to provide a scapegoat for the structure that masquerades as the only liberal democracy in the region.

We can see this scapegoating in how some Western governments have responded to settlement expansion. For example, both Nachala and Weiss have been sanctioned by the UK, Australia, Canada and the European Union – sanctions that include asset freezes and travel bans. Sanctions like this effectively allow governments to claim action, when in reality, the impact on the ground is limited.

This distinction between settlers and the Israeli regime is also evident in the language used to announce the sanctions. In her November 18 statement announcing the sanctions, Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong failed to mention the Israeli government at all: “We are taking these actions because the rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution”.

Some might argue that freezing settler assets and imposing travel bans is at least a step in the right direction. But this is a naive outlook. Limited sanctions like these are a politically calculated tactic. In the UK, growing anger among the British public over their government’s complicity in the genocide necessitated a response from the incoming prime minister, Andy Burnham.

Yet when his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced earlier this year the new approach the UK government was taking vis-à-vis Palestine and Israel, it was reported that British officials were also working to de-escalate tensions and give assurances to the Israeli government that the sanctions would be limited in scope.

Indeed, the earlier sanctions did nothing to stop what happened in al-Duyuk at-Tahta, where Palestinians were evicted from their homes by settlers, supported by soldiers and praised by government ministers. In fact, the settler movement appears to be intact and growing in support and power every day.

This is why sanctions cannot be limited to individual actors and organisations – they need to be comprehensively applied to the structure behind them. But that requires a moral backbone and political courage – something that seems to be completely lacking on the international stage.

articles.title: 'Police have no regard for life, liberty': MP high court slams DGP Kailash Makwana, Gwalior SSP over 31 of 34 unanswered requisitions in prisoner's bail case; reserve inspector, constable suspended
articles.summary: BHOPAL: The Madhya Pradesh high court has come down heavily on senior police officers, including the state DGP and Gwalior SSP, over alleged suppression
articles.body: BHOPAL: The Madhya Pradesh high court has come down heavily on senior police officers, including the state DGP and Gwalior SSP, over alleged suppression of facts and failure to act on official communications concerning a prisoner's bail plea.The court questioned whether senior police officers had verified the records before submitting comments and accused the police hierarchy of attempting to shield those responsible for the lapses.A division bench of justice GS Ahluwalia and justice Anuradha Shukla, in an order passed on November 26, expressed serious concern over the police department's conduct, observing that its senior officers appeared to have little regard for the life and liberty of prisoners or the law.The case relates to a criminal appeal filed by Ramjeet alias Ramjilal and others. During the proceedings, the court examined 34 requisitions received by a reserve inspector in connection with the matter. Only three were answered, while the remaining 31 were allegedly left unattended.The court noted that the communications were available in the reserve inspector's records. It questioned how DGP Kailash Makwana could submit comments claiming there was no basis to infer apathy on the part of the police department when 31 requisitions remained unanswered.The bench also observed that the DGP's comments were neither signed by him nor accompanied by an affidavit. When it considered issuing notice to the DGP, Gwalior SSP Dharmveer Singh told the court that senior officers, including the in-charge DIG, had verified the records but had not informed the DGP about the unanswered requisitions.The SSP further submitted that the comments filed before the high court had been approved by the DGP.Questioning this explanation, the bench observed that either the DGP was aware of the correct facts or had endorsed the police department's conduct without verifying the records.The court also questioned the basis for the DGP's comments in light of the SSP's decision to order a preliminary inquiry and seek a month's time to examine the matter.Appearing before the court, the SSP said he had suspended Reserve Inspector Ranjeet Singh Sikarwar and a constable. He later sought time to explain his decision to order a preliminary inquiry, saying he had been undergoing training and was unaware of the case details.The bench rejected this explanation, observing that the relevant facts had already been set out in its earlier orders and that the SSP was aware of the developments.In another serious development, the court flagged irregularities in the handling of official documents by the office of the additional advocate general.It noted that comments sought from the DGP had been shown to the court on November 16, with an assurance that they would be filed the same day. However, they were submitted only on November 23.The court also found that a compliance report shown on November 25 and cleared for filing by the regular Reader, Hariom Sharma, had not been uploaded to the court's electronic portal.On examining the physical file, the bench found that Mohd Sabir, a substitute Reader, had struck out the earlier permission and granted fresh permission on November 26.The bench issued a show-cause notice to Sabir, asking him to explain why he had altered the permission without the court's approval. Sabir accepted the notice and sought a week's time to respond.The court warned the office of the additional advocate general against retaining documents after showing them to the bench and obtaining permission to file them.Taking note of the SSP's submission that the two suspended personnel would not be reinstated until the departmental inquiry was completed, the court recorded his undertaking.The bench directed that a copy of its order be sent to the chief minister and chief secretary of Madhya Pradesh. articles.title: Italy's former police chief rejected mafia inquiry allegations before death
articles.summary: The contents of an eight-page letter by Gianni De Gennaro have been revealed days after his body was found at his Tuscany home.
articles.body:
Italian ex-police chief Gianni De Gennaro has denied misleading investigations into high-profile Mafia killings, in a letter written shortly before his death.

His body was found at his Tuscan country home on Saturday and Italian authorities believe he took his own life. A post mortem examination was due to take place on Friday.

In his eight-page note, De Gennaro, 78, vehemently denied obstructing the inquiry into the murder of anti-mafia judge Paolo Borsellino in Sicily in July 1992.

The Cosa Nostra Mafia was found to have ordered Borsellino's killing and that of fellow judge Giovanni Falcone two months earlier.

But several fruitless investigations were later launched into potential cover-ups by high-ranking officials.

In a recent inquiry De Gennaro, who in the 1990s worked in the anti-mafia directorate and later became Italy's police chief, was accused of misdirecting the initial investigation.

The allegations shocked many Italians, as De Gennaro had worked closely with Falcone and was seen as being on the front line of the fight against organised crime.

"In a few minutes I will be gone, so you understand well that a 'man condemned to death' cannot lie," he wrote in the letter, published by Italian daily Corriere della Sera. "I have never betrayed my oath of loyalty to the Fatherland."

"I hope that, amid the avalanche of falsehoods now overwhelming me, the truth will ultimately prevail," he added.

The case, and the media furore that has surrounded it, have re-opened the wound of the Mafia killings of the early 1990s, which remain an emotionally charged issue in Italy.

The story has dominated Italian headlines since De Gennaro's death, with several of the country's most senior political figures publicly commenting on the case.

On Thursday Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she had been "deeply shocked" by the case.

"His words struck us deeply, and I think the most important think we can do now is to help prosecutors who are working to clear things up," she added.

The letter, which De Gennaro reportedly headlined "My moral testament", was found next to a hard drive which he said contained notes from his 40-year career.

According to Italian media, investigators seized two hard drives, one from the home of De Gennaro's son and one from a former member of his security detail, and two USB sticks held by a close collaborator, who is also under investigation.

The sticks are reportedly labelled "Stato-Mafia", a likely reference to the alleged relationship between the Italian state and the Mafia, and "Massacres".

Forensic specialists are now expected to examine whether any files on the hard drives or USB sticks were altered or deleted, reports say.

articles.title: In 1982, Seiko put a Seiko TV in a watch with a 1.2-inch screen, but watching it meant carrying a separate receiver in your pocket
articles.summary: Discover the remarkable story of Seiko's 1982 TV watch, the world's first wristwatch with a television tuner and headphone jack, and explore its innovative technology and design impact.
articles.body: Sneaking a look at a screen in a boring meeting might feel like a modern habit, but in 1982, Seiko tried to do just that with a TV on the wrist. The Seiko Museum Ginza describes the 1982 LCD TV watch as the world's first watch with a tuner and a headphone jack, made for watching TV anywhere, anytime. It had a 1.2-inch screen and was worn on the wrist like a digital watch. However, there was a catch: the wearer had to carry a separate receiver in a pocket to watch anything.A tiny screen packed with new technologyThe TV screen was 1.2 inches large and had a liquid crystal display, which was a pretty big deal for its time. The museum says it had an advanced LSI chip and liquid crystal technology that was instantly responsive to low voltage. This means that the screen could display moving pictures while requiring very little energy. The watch could still perform basic tasks like the alarm, chronograph, calendar and also tune in to FM radio. Seiko Epson's company history adds that the display was built from a panel first created for watches but modified to display moving images. At the time, the manufacturing company was Suwa Seikosha, and the TV watch was launched under the Seiko brand in December 1982, after being announced earlier that year.Why the pocket was importantThe screen on the wrist was only half the story. The Smithsonian Institution's Smithsonian Insider explains that the TV watch needed a receiver and battery pack, both carried in a separate bag or pocket. A cable ran through the sleeve of a jacket and connected the receiver to the wrist screen. The same cable also served as the TV aerial. A headpiece was also needed for the sound, so this tiny TV was really a small kit, not just a watch. Seiko Epson says the TV consumed less power than any before it and could run up to five hours on two AA batteries.A record breaker that did not catch onAlthough the gadget was heavier thanks to all the additional equipment, the TV watch was still very well received. Seiko Epson says it won the Nikkei Award for Superior Products and Services in 1982. The 1984 edition of the Guinness Book of World Records recognised the device as the world's smallest television. As for sales, that was another story. The Smithsonian Insider reported that the product appeared in the U.S. market in 1983 for $500. Carlene Stephens, a watch curator at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History, says it did not really catch on. In her opinion, the watch itself was not that big, but people didn't like carrying the battery pack around. A gadget that needed a cable up a sleeve and a box in a pocket was a pretty hard sell.Why the idea still mattersToday, more powerful screens sit in pockets and on wrists. Stephens says the wrist is a spot manufacturers find it hard to resist because it is personal, easy to use and always available. She also notes that the Apple Watch was not the first attempt to put the latest tech on the wrist, and she uses Seiko's TV watch as one of her examples. It was an attractive idea in itself, even if the equipment around it was pretty elaborate. But as a piece of design history, that tiny screen on the wrist can be a nice reminder of just how far portable tech has come.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Around 60 Maryland landowners approach US Supreme Court to challenge a proposed 67-mile power line project; residents argue that a private energy company cannot enter their properties for surveys
articles.summary: Around 60 Maryland landowners have approached the US Supreme Court in an effort to stop a private energy company from entering their properties to conduct
articles.body: Around 60 Maryland landowners have approached the US Supreme Court in an effort to stop a private energy company from entering their properties to conduct surveys for a proposed 67-mile electricity transmission line. The petition challenges lower court decisions that allowed PSEG Renewable Transmission to access private land before its authority to do so was established. The dispute centres on property rights, the use of eminent domain and whether a company can obtain court-ordered access while its proposed infrastructure project is still awaiting state approval.Maryland landowners challenged the 67-mile power line projectThe dispute involves the Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project (MPRP), a proposed transmission line that would pass through rural parts of Baltimore, Carroll and Frederick counties. The project is being developed by PSEG Renewable Transmission, a New Jersey-based energy company.According to Maryland Matters, 60 landowners filed a petition with the US Supreme Court on November 4, challenging decisions that allowed PSEG surveyors to enter their properties for field studies. The landowners are represented without charge by the Pacific Legal Foundation.The residents argue that PSEG should not be permitted to enter privately owned land until it has secured the necessary approval from Maryland regulators and established that it has the legal authority to exercise eminent domain.Eminent domain is the power that allows government authorities, and certain legally authorised entities, to acquire or access private property for public projects under specific conditions. The landowners' objection is that PSEG has been allowed to exercise powers associated with this authority without first demonstrating that it qualifies.How the legal dispute reached the Supreme CourtThe disagreement has been developing for several years, with resistance from property owners along the proposed transmission line route.In April 2025, PSEG filed a lawsuit against more than 100 landowners who had refused to allow survey teams onto their properties. The company maintained that Maryland law permitted entities with eminent domain authority to enter private land to collect information needed for proposed infrastructure projects.In June 2025, US District Court Judge Adam Abelson granted PSEG a preliminary injunction, allowing its surveyors to enter the disputed properties despite opposition from residents. A preliminary injunction is a temporary court order that permits or prevents certain actions while a legal dispute is being considered.The landowners subsequently challenged the decision, but the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit upheld the injunction in August 2026. As reported by FOX45 News, the appeals court decided that PSEG likely possessed the necessary eminent domain authority to conduct surveys before receiving its final state approval.The court's reasoning was linked to Maryland's regulatory process, which requires field studies and other technical information before the Public Service Commission can decide whether to approve the project.The landowners now want the Supreme Court to examine whether that reasoning allowed a private company to exercise disputed property access rights prematurely.The project raised concerns about data centre expansionBeyond the immediate disagreement over access to private land, the transmission line has become part of a wider debate about the growing demand for electricity from data centres in the region.The Washington Times, in its November 8 report, connected the landowners' Supreme Court challenge to concerns about the expansion of data centres in the metropolitan area. Residents argue that the proposed transmission infrastructure will help supply electricity to an increasing number of these facilities, which require substantial amounts of power to operate.The need for additional electricity has also been highlighted by regional grid operator PJM Interconnection. According to Maryland Matters, PJM considers the MPRP necessary to prevent problems with the region's electricity infrastructure, including potential blackouts. This comes as electricity demand from data centres continues to rise while some existing power plants are being retired.Survey access has already affected landownersAccording to Maryland Matters, PSEG's fieldwork has included boundary surveys, assessments of forests and wetlands, habitat studies and acoustic surveys to identify bats. The company reported in September 2026 that only 9 archaeological surveys remained on properties involved in the original lawsuit.FOX45 News also reported that the dispute extended beyond permission to conduct surveys. PSEG sought additional restrictions preventing landowners from hunting on their properties during notified surveying periods.In one example detailed in the court petition, survey notices covered the period from September 29 to October 31, 2025, even though a land agent reportedly indicated that the actual survey work would require only one day. A federal judge granted restrictions requiring property owners to obtain written agreement from PSEG before hunting during those periods.According to FOX45 News, the Supreme Court has not yet agreed to hear the case. Meanwhile, the Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project(MPRP) remains under the state's regulatory review process.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Apple AirTag leads firefighters to cat stuck in narrow gap between cement walls
articles.summary: Firefighters drilled through concrete to free a missing cat tracked by an Apple AirTag in California, reuniting the feline with its owner.
articles.body: Firefighters in Southern California rescued a missing cat wedged in a narrow gap between two concrete walls after the pet was tracked to the location thanks to an Apple AirTag on its collar. The orange-and-white feline was stuck in a 4 to 5-inch-wide gap between two 8-foot-tall retaining walls in Indian Wells, the Riverside County Fire Department said on social media. The owner located the missing cat using an AirTag attached to its collar, and firefighters were then able to free the animal from the tight spot. TEXAS FIREFIGHTERS RESCUE DISTRESSED RACCOON AFTER ITS HEAD GETS STUCK IN A HOLE IN A TREE With help from Riverside County Animal Services, "firefighters used specialized equipment to gain access through the wall and safely extricate the cat," the fire department said. "Great teamwork by all involved in bringing this furry family member to safety!" the post added. The cat was then reunited with its owner and transported to an emergency veterinarian for medical treatment. A MISSING KITTEN RODE UNDER A CAR HOOD. AI BROUGHT HER HOME Video posted by the fire department showed a firefighter drilling into a concrete wall before pulling the cat free and lifting it out of the wall. Images also show a firefighter holding the cat after it was rescued from the gap. It was unclear how the animal managed to get stuck in the narrow gap. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP While the AirTag was used as a useful tool to rescue the cat, Apple typically does not recommend using the device for tracking pets. Apple wrote on its website in January, while announcing the release of the new AirTag, that the device is designed "exclusively for tracking objects, and not people or pets."

articles.title: New Zealand election results set up tricky talks for conservative incumbent
articles.summary: Conservative PM Luxon and populist coalition partners face negotiations with centrist kingmaker.
articles.body:
The final results of New Zealand’s November 7 election offer no clear path to forming a government, suggesting tricky political wrangling is likely in the weeks ahead.

The results, released on Friday, showed that the ruling centre-right coalition led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s conservative National Party has fallen one seat short of a parliamentary majority.

Luxon has led New Zealand since 2023, but National and its junior partners – the populist New Zealand First and libertarian ACT – won just 65 seats between them. National secured 40 seats while ACT and New Zealand First won 13 seats and 12 seats, respectively.

The result reflects a loss of support for Luxon driven by a stagnant economy, and leaves the former businessman and his coalition partners to seek additional help to secure a majority.

“New Zealanders need a government that is stable, that works together and will last for the full term,” Luxon told a news conference on Friday.

Labour, the largest opposition party, won 36 seats, leaving it far below the 66-seat threshold in the 130-member parliament.

The results appear to position Qiulae Wong’s centrist Opportunity Party, which clinched 7 seats, as kingmaker. However, talks with the conservative and populist incumbents are likely to prove tricky.

The former consultant has promised a universal basic income of up to NZ$370 (US$208) a week, greater action on climate change, a ban on bottom-trawling fishing, and healthcare reforms.

She has also campaigned for a kinder approach to politics. Wong has pledged to do “everything we can” to ensure a stable government.

Her style contrasts with that of potential suitors such as Winston Peters of New Zealand First. The controversial foreign minister has called opponents “morons” and drew shock earlier this year when he told a Chinese-born lawmaker to “go back to your country”. His party promises to tighten immigration flows and withdraw from the Paris Climate Accord.

Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour of ACT campaigned against a greater governance role for the Indigenous Maori minority and has promised massive cuts to state spending.

Failure to meet an agreement could see Kiwis return to the polls next year.

Luke Oldfield, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, told Reuters news agency a deal was likely, although it could be challenging.

“I don’t know exactly what kind of shape that will be yet, but it’ll be highly likely that there will be a right bloc formed and not a second election,” he said.

articles.title: Diljit Dosanjh's Mumbai concert today: 500+ cops, bomb squads and no-car zone after threat email; MNS seeks ban on racecourse shows over drugs
articles.summary: MUMBAI: With more than 500 police personnel, bomb detection teams and a strict no-car zone, actor-singer Diljit Dosanjh's concert at Mahalaxmi Racecourse
articles.body: MUMBAI: With more than 500 police personnel, bomb detection teams and a strict no-car zone, actor-singer Diljit Dosanjh's concert at Mahalaxmi Racecourse on Friday is taking place under heightened security after a threat email warned of possible attacks on the venue and Metro stations.But security is not the only controversy surrounding the show; the Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) has demanded a ban on concerts at the racecourse and NSCI Dome, alleging that such events have become hubs for drug use and civic disruption.The threat email, received on Thursday, the anniversary of the 26/11 terror attacks, warned of blasts, grenade attacks and improvised explosive devices at the mayor's office, Metro stations and Dosanjh's concert.The sender identified herself as Hannah Meler and referred to Khalistan and the 1984 anti-Sikh riots, besides threatening violence linked to a programme involving the singer and people associated with the event.Following the threat, Mumbai Police have stepped up security at Mahalaxmi Racecourse, where Dosanjh is scheduled to perform as part of his RuPay AURA India Tour 2026.500+ personnel, five entry gates and a no-car zoneMore than 500 police personnel will be deployed at the venue, including around 200 constables, 150 women constables and 75 officers, along with personnel in plain clothes stationed around the singer. Dog squads and an Anti-Narcotics Cell (ANC) team will also be present.Bomb Detection and Disposal Squad teams have swept the venue, while entry checks will be conducted at all five gates instead of the earlier three. Private security personnel have also been engaged to assist the police.A no-car zone extending 500 to 700 metres around the racecourse will be enforced, and parking will not be allowed at the event. No road diversions have been announced so far.Organisers have also been instructed not to disclose details of the singer's hotel or arrival time. Posters, banners, signs and flags of any kind have been barred inside the venue.MNS wants concerts at Mahalaxmi Racecourse, NSCI Dome stoppedEven as the city prepares for the concert, the MNS has written to Mumbai Police seeking an immediate and permanent ban on live music concerts and large-scale entertainment events at Mahalaxmi Racecourse and the NSCI Dome.The party has cited alleged drug use, traffic congestion and the death of a young man at a concert venue last year.In a letter to the police, MNS leader Dinesh Dnyaneshwar Punde claimed that drugs were openly sold and consumed at such events, putting young people at risk. He cited a November 22 event at which the ANC reportedly booked 12-13 people for drug consumption, and referred to an earlier fatal incident involving a young man.The letter also flagged traffic congestion caused by concerts, saying it created difficulties for local residents. Punde warned that MNS workers and residents would stage a road blockade if permissions for such events continued to be granted.Police step up anti-drug checks at concert venuesThe MNS demand comes amid increased scrutiny of drug use at large events. Earlier this week, Mumbai Police deployed a newly launched ANC forensic van outside Mahalaxmi Racecourse as part of efforts to curb narcotics use.The mobile unit is equipped with five rapid detection machines and 360-degree surveillance cameras. These include TruNarc, which uses Raman laser technology to identify narcotic substances without opening their packaging; Gemini, which can identify a wider range of substances, including narcotics, hazardous chemicals and explosives; and the Dräger DrugTest 5000, which detects drug consumption through oral swab testing.The police said the equipment would help personnel identify substances and detect drug consumption at event venues.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: In 1975, an Ohio couple collected 1,400 cans for a homemade solar furnace; sunlight warmed their home into the 70s, with oil heat used after the sun went down
articles.summary: Explore how an Ohio couple created a homemade solar furnace from 1,400 cans in 1975, reducing their reliance on oil heat and embracing solar energy during a time of energy crisis.
articles.body: In 1975, an Ohio couple gathered 1,400 cans to build a homemade solar furnace. According to a 1977 issue of The Worldwide News, sunlight warmed their home into the 70s Fahrenheit, or about 21 degrees to 26 degrees Celsius. Oil heat was used only after sunset. It might sound like some quirky experiment, but it reflects a time when ordinary households were looking for ways to keep their homes warm without relying on oil alone.Why homes were turning to the sunThe mid-1970s saw some tense years for energy markets. Yale University's Energy History website explained how the oil prices of 1973 and 1974 led to the price of gasoline and crude oil quadrupling. This was a source of concern for the future of energy in the nation. Solar power was seen as one of the more promising solutions for the future since it could be produced and used at the scale of a single home. In this context, the couple’s decision to collect cans to harness solar energy was part of a wider search for new answers.Sunshine by day, oil after darkThe most interesting part of the couple's story was how practical it was. The sun warmed the house into the 70s, and oil heat was used only after the sun had gone down. The oil system was not completely abandoned; it was a reserve for when there was no sun. This kind of mix makes sense, as the sun can't heat a home in the dark. The homemade furnace didn’t have to do all the work alone. It could take over the daytime work while oil covered the rest.What NASA engineers found about solar heatingHome solar heating was also receiving attention from experts. A technical memorandum from NASA's Langley Research Center outlined a low-cost solar heating system designed to supplement a homeowner's existing warm-air heating system. Tests of a demonstration system indicated that a homeowner could save about 40% of the heating costs if they had a 1,500-square-foot home with insulation to the 1974 FHA minimum standards. The figure applies to NASA's design and not to the furnace owned by the Ohio couple. The memorandum also added that homeowners couldn’t just choose a solar heating system from stock at a local heating contractor. This gap may help explain why some households tried to build their own systems.Why one success story has limitsAn important note of caution came from Yale’s Energy History website. Despite the high hopes, it observed solar energy in the 1970s had critical limitations. Many solar technologies were still highly experimental, small in scale, and unconventional in design, so the Ohio couple's result was a hopeful example, not a guarantee. Sunlight, house size, and insulation all play a role in how well a heating system performs. So results from one home cannot be assumed for another.What the story still teachesToday, energy bills and climate worries are familiar topics for many young adults. So this story, more than 50 years later, still feels relevant. The couple saw an opportunity, gathered materials, and tried to find a practical solution. They also used oil heat after sunset instead of relying on the sun alone. The story shows how major changes in home heating can often begin with small experiments using something as simple as a can.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
